entries.title: UN food program cuts aid to 500,000 Palestinians in Gaza
entries.summary: Amid funding shortages, the World Food Program has said it is being forced to reduce necessary aid. Over two-thirds of Palestinians in Gaza are facing acute hunger, according to the agency.
entries.content:
Palestinian Territories

UN food program cuts aid to 500,000 Palestinians in Gaza

October 19, 2026

Amid funding shortages, the World Food Program has said it is being forced to reduce necessary aid. Over two-thirds of Palestinians in Gaza are facing acute hunger, according to the agency.

The United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) has been forced to cut its monthly food aid to the war-ravaged Gaza Strip , where some two-thirds of the population are struggling to get food, the agency said on Monday.

The WFP said it was reducing the number of people receiving aid from 1.6 million to 1.1 million, leaving some 500,000 people without support.

The UN program is facing severe funding shortages. "WFP no longer has sufficient funding to sustain this level of support," the organization said.

What UN aid is being cut in Gaza?

Beyond the cutting of aid to some half a million recipients in the region, the WFP is also:

  • Reducing rations by half
  • Cash assistance has been cut for some 75,000 families
  • Hot meals for those unable to cook have been reduced from 250,000 to 150,000

Some 1.4 million people in Gaza are facing crisis levels of food insecurity according to the WFP, with 200,000 living in emergency conditions.

Despite a US-brokered ceasefire that came into effect last year, Israeli strikes have continued and aid has remained restricted, with little progress toward a final end to the conflict.

"It's a year into the agreement of this ceasefire. Well, life is still brutal here. There is no proper shelter. There is no ⁠basic ​services. There is no safety, no security," acting Executive ​Director of the World Food Program WFP Carl Skau told Reuters in Gaza.

"These cuts are happening ​just as we are facing the fourth winter. You know, I've been through the winters here, absolutely brutal," he added.

Why is aid being cut to Gaza?

The UN program urgently needs $450 million (€400 million) to keep funding its critical operations in Gaza and the West Bank over the next six months.

"We tell the world now ⁠is not ​the time to look away. This is the time to step up to sustain this support, to protect the progress that has been made, but also to push for early recovery," Skau said.

The WFP had already announced cuts to aid for the West Bank in early September, citing funding shortages and donor fatigue.

The Israeli authority responsible for the Palestinian territories, COGAT, says the supply of aid deliveries into the strip exceeds the demand for food and it claims there is no acute food insecurity in Gaza.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: From delivery driver to global fame: A Korean writer's journey
entries.summary: You Yeong-Gwang's The Rainfall Market tells the story of a mysterious, hidden shop that only opens when it rains. For a debut novel by an unknown author, it was a massive success.
entries.content:
October 19, 2026

You Yeong-Gwang's The Rainfall Market tells the story of a mysterious, hidden shop that only opens when it rains. For a debut novel by an unknown author, it was a massive success.

For ten years, publishers rejected You Yeong-Gwang's book. Yet before it was even printed in South Korea, the once-abandoned manuscript had international publishers flocking to secure translation rights.  

"I'm so grateful that the book has now been published in more than 20 countries. Even more astonishingly, it also appeared on the Der Spiegel bestseller list in Germany," he told DW while attending the 2026 Frankfurt Book Fair.

For a debut novel by an unknown author, it was a massive success, securing publication in 15 languages, including English, German, Spanish and traditional Chinese.

"The Rainfall Market" tells the story of a mysterious, hidden shop that only opens when it rains. In the shop, visitors can exchange their deepest unhappiness for a ticket to a brand-new destiny. The plot revolves around Serin, a disheartened young girl who stumbles into the marketplace run by whimsical spirits, finding a warm, comforting space.

"In fact, Serin's story is my story," author You said. "For a long time, I even wondered how wonderful it would be if I could sell my unhappiness and use the money to buy happiness."

While writing the book, he was going through a difficult time himself.

"I had to care for my mother, who had been ill for a long time, and I had also been responsible for supporting my family financially for many years. Life felt incredibly heavy," he reflected.

"But when I was writing, I could immerse myself in the world of the story and, even if only for a short while, forget about those circumstances. That's why writing made me so happy. I truly enjoyed it."

On the creation of 'The Rainfall Market'

The idea of rain is inspired by his own life.

"At that time, my circumstances felt as though it were raining constantly," You said.

The story draws heavily on traditional Korean folklore, serving as a quintessential "healing fiction" tale in which its young protagonist must weigh the true cost of seemingly perfect lives.

"When I was writing, I wasn't consciously trying to write healing fiction. At the time, I didn't even really know that such a label existed."

He initially planned to publish a book independently and started crowdfunding. But as the funding failed, he used all his savings and printed 200 copies, which bookstores refused to take. In a month, he only sold five copies. "I thought that's it. I really have to give up now.”

"At the time, I had undergone eye surgery and due to complications, I couldn't see, so I started working at a call center, where I could work using my voice." You said. "During the week, I worked at a call center, and on weekends I went to a computer academy. I learned how to make books on my own for a few years."

He then taught himself how to use the software needed to create books on his own.

While running one of the crowdfunding campaigns, he started working as a food delivery driver. "The round trip between my home and the area where I delivered food took about four hours each day. So I wrote on my phone's memo app while traveling on the subway."

"Even when I was going through very difficult circumstances, I was able to keep writing because the moments when I was writing were so joyful. For a little while, I could forget about the difficult situation I was in," You explained.

Finally a breakthrough

"I gathered those pieces of writing together and launched what I intended to be my final crowdfunding campaign," he said.

The campaign was intended to fund the publication of "The Rainfall Market."

"To my amazement, the campaign succeeded, and I was able to publish the book commercially for the first time," he said.

Following the crowdfunding success, the novel was acquired by Clayhouse, a prominent South Korean publishing company.

Before it was even published, he had received offers from publishers in five countries and signed international publishing contracts.

And in the first month after publication, the book sold 30,000 copies across all formats, ranking as the bestselling e-book and third-bestselling physical book.

"I still find it hard to believe that all of this has happened and that I'm here at the Frankfurt Book Fair. I'm incredibly grateful and happy," said You.

A new horizon for Hallyu, or the 'Korean Wave': K-Comfort Fiction

Korea's newest soft power is K-literature, which sold about 1.2 million translated copies abroad in 2025 for the second consecutive year.

And You's book belongs to a trending genre called Korean comfort fiction.

"When readers closed the book, I wanted them to feel a little warmth in their hearts," he said.

Although Korean literature was first known for darker, more pragmatic books about societal realities, K-comfort fiction is the child of South Korea's pressure-cooker modern society. It offers an answer to the human need for escapism and a transient antidote to the reality of a hyper-competitive education system, brutal job market, and intense corporate pressure. 

"When I was writing, I was going through a very difficult time myself, and I wished someone would comfort me. So, I thought, why don't I try reading something like that myself? Why don't I write something that can comfort me?" You wondered.

With burnout on the rise globally, more readers are seeking soul-soothing literature with exhausted protagonists they can relate to. Usually without a need to defeat a villain, the stories follow protagonists with a deep desire for rest, community and emotional repair.

The whimsical fiction aspect is the missing element allowing them to step away from reality. The genre originally gained traction through indie productions, online crowdfunding and endorsements from high-profile K-pop artists.

Despite the Korean context, this style of storytelling quickly went global, capturing different international audiences, including those already familiar with cozy K-dramas or those simply looking for a gentle refuge from the anxieties of the modern world.

Last year, the bestselling Korean novel abroad was Welcome to the Hyunam-dong Bookshop, according to the Literature Translation Institute of Korea. This book also belongs to the same genre as The Rainfall Market.

While readers embrace the genre, critics view it with literary skepticism. They point out that it relies heavily on a predictable, repetitive formula, often built around a single magical space, with simplistic prose and low-stakes conflicts that prioritize cozy vibes over deep character development.

Reviewing The Rainfall Market for the Korea Times, Peter Juhl, a literary critic, described healing fiction as light, feel-good stories and argued the boom reflects a deliberate effort to write global novels for international markets.

On his future aspirations and message to readers

"Of course, I'm happy that my book is receiving so much love and that I'm able to write. But more than anything, I hope my mother gets better and regains her health," he said after mentioning that his mother underwent surgery a week before his arrival at the book fair.

Beyond the book itself, people seem to relate to and appreciate the story of his own life.

"If I have the opportunity, I'd like to share more stories about hope and dreams with people who are going through circumstances similar to mine," said You. "If my story can help one person even a little, in any way, I don't think anything could make me happier."

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

entries.title: The homeless man living in front of a London mega-mansion
entries.summary: Anders Fernstedt lives in London without any money. The Swedish native has built a most unusual home under the porch of a house worth over €200 million. How did that happen?
entries.content:
October 19, 2026

Anders Fernstedt lives in London without any money. The Swedish native has built a most unusual home under the porch of a house worth over €200 million. How did that happen?

There's a lot of stopping and staring in Knightsbridge. This part of central London is within a stone's throw of Buckingham Palace, Hyde Park and Harrods, bringing inquisitive tourists in droves.

While it may not divert quite as many eyeballs as the seat of the British monarchy, a curious collection of plants, garden umbrellas, shopping bags and children's toys filling a building's entrance causes many a curious glance.

The peculiar arrangement on a grand portico is what Anders Fernstedt, a man from Sweden who fell on hard times, has been calling home for more than three years already.

That building hosting his makeshift setup was, just a few years ago, London's most expensive house.

The mega-mansion at 2-8A Rutland Gate sold in 2020 for a then-record £210 million (€244 million, $278 million) to Hui Ka Yan, the founder of China's Evergrande group, who was sentenced to life in prison last month.

Hui never moved in and the house was registered under his wife's name. The freezing of her assets means it can't be seized by liquidators and the house is in a state of limbo.

So too was Fernstedt when he first stumbled across it. "I just thought, it would be a shelter for the night. I'm an avid camper, like an amateur botanist. I'm not afraid of nature," he told DW.

'Camping on the balcony'

Fernstedt has never been inside the property, which appears to be in a state of disrepair. Instead, he gradually built his home in the portico, where grand columns guard the 45 rooms, indoor swimming pool and 116 windows. Year round he sleeps under the portico roof and a large umbrella which provides a hidden nook in which he's placed mattresses and bedding.

"I haven't had a bad night's sleep for as long as I can remember. And that goes for four seasons. It's not cold in the winter, and because I don't have walls, I get the breeze in the heat," he said.

"My conceit when I started was that sort of fake dream. Oh, I'm just a boy, my parents are in the house, everything's normal, I just asked them for permission to camp on the balcony."

Fernstedt was raised by his mother in Sweden before embarking on a range of careers at home and in the US, building a name for himself in the tech world.

In 2016, he moved to England where he worked as a journalist and fact checker at publications including The Economist, before work dried up around the time of the COVID pandemic.

A share in a tech company from his days in the US gave Anders a nest egg he relied on. But it couldn't last forever and he found himself living in a tent and then temporary accommodation, where he experienced violence and brushed up against people with severe addictions.

"Perhaps in this contemporary world, the biggest curiosity about my lifestyle is I'm completely off money," he said.

Community support powers unusual lifestyle

Fernstedt has built relationships with bakeries, cafes and florists in which he gets unused food, flowers for his home and use of power. He also makes use of a homeless charity in nearby Victoria for showers, clothing donations and socializing. But he's also made himself a broadly accepted part of one of London's most affluent neighborhoods.

"This is a very sophisticated neighborhood. I'd stayed for a few weeks and I knew everybody knew that I was here. And I thought, how can I sort of convey my presence without being present? And I thought, my constituency has to be the neighbors' children and grandchildren. Because if they plead my case at the kitchen table, my prospects improve," he said, by way of explaining the toys that line his abode.

"It is, in a way, a squirrel's nut collection," he added, when asked if he's worried about leaving his possessions out in the open. "I have so many nuts that I won't notice when something disappears."

There are some neighbors who do object to his presence, but Anders does his best to keep his home neat and his life quiet. Indeed, many others feel his presence prevents the house being a target for thieves or vandals. Overall though, he's found the community welcoming.

"Sometimes they introduce themselves asking what might I want or need. And my stock answer being: 'well, what you just gave me, a little bit of normal time, right? And neighborly banter'," he said. "Sometimes I'll be given food and very elegant Italian dinner jackets and clothes have arrived on a few occasions."

Homelessness a growing concern in London

Not all homeless people in London have found such a stable lifestyle. Homeless charity Crisis estimates that there are over 200,000 people classified as homeless in England's capital, where "4,392 people were recorded sleeping rough in London between April and June, up from 4% on the same time last year. This is up 58% compared to 10 years ago."

According to government figures, there were 105,138 empty homes in London in 2025, or 1 in every 37 homes. Andy Burnham, who became British Prime Minister in July, has since vowed to offer "every rough sleeper in England a route off the streets by Christmas." 

With such an enormous price tag, even after six years of being abandoned, Fernstedt knows that the house he lives at could potentially become untenable at virtually any moment.

But over the last few years, it's given him something he craved when pitching up his tent or being moved from one scary temporary residence to the next.

"I'm no longer really worried that I'll cycle around the corner and everything will be gone. Because I've been here so long, I'm free of worrying now, and if we worry too much, we won't be happy."

Edited by: Elizabeth Grenier

entries.title: Greece: At least 12 die in migrant drownings overnight
entries.summary: Authorities say 12 people, including an infant, have drowned in Greek waters in two separate incidents overnight. Another 22 people were rescued. A search-and-rescue operation is ongoing.
entries.content:
October 19, 2026

Authorities say 12 people, including an infant, have drowned in Greek waters in two separate incidents overnight. Another 22 people were rescued. A search-and-rescue operation is ongoing.

Greek Coast Guard officials say 12 migrants were killed in the Aegean Sea overnight in two separate boating accidents.

In the first incident, six people — four men, a woman and an infant — were killed in waters off the coast of Lesbos when "a speedboat carrying migrants collided with the port side of a police patrol vessel," according to the Coast Guard.

Eight people were reported rescued.

In the second incident, six people — five men and a woman — drowned after their boat capsized off the coast of Samos, while 14 were rescued.

A search-and-rescue mission is ongoing in the area.

Authorities say they arrested a 37-year-old Turkish national among the survivors in the first incident, identifying him ‌as ​a suspected smuggler and the operator of the speedboat.

Greece's Minister of Shipping and Island Policy Vassilis Kikilias blamed migrant traffickers for all of the deaths, posting on X, "Our position is non-negotiable: Zero tolerance for smugglers."

Turkey to Greece: Deadly migrant passage to Europe

Greece has long been a gateway ​to Europe for migrants and ⁠refugees from the Middle East, Africa and Asia who usually set off on the notoriously deadly sea voyage from Turkey.

According to the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), refugee arrivals in Greece are declining this year.

As of October 11, 2026, some 25,000 arrivals had been recorded compared to 42,000 in 2025.

Almost one million migrants and refugees landed on Greece's shores during the 2015/2016 migration crisis, here, too, mainly from Turkey.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: Australian MP seriously hurt in suspected car attack
entries.summary: Helen Haines, an independent federal lawmaker, has been struck by a car in what Australia's prime minister has called an apparent attack.
entries.content:
Australia

Australian MP Helen Haines seriously hurt in suspected car attack

October 19, 2026

Helen Haines, an independent federal lawmaker, has been struck by a car in what Australia's prime minister has called an apparent attack.

Australian police are investigating a suspected car attack that has left independent MP Helen Haines with critical injuries.

Counterterrorism investigators have joined the probe following the incident, which occurred outside Haines' constituency office in Wangaratta, northeast of the Victorian capital, Melbourne.

What do we know about the suspected attack on Haines?

Haines, 65, was hit by an SUV, said by police to be a white Toyota, outside her office, leaving her with serious injuries, particularly to her lower body.

Broadcaster ABC cited witnesses as saying they had heard a bang and then saw a woman pinned between two cars.

The driver, described as a 43-year-old man, has been arrested, according to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese.

Investigators are reported to have found a knife in the car.

Apparently deliberate attack: PM Albanese

"This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear," Albanese told ABC.

He said it was too early to speculate about the possible motive behind the suspected attack, but pointed to rising political violence.

"The temperature has increased in recent times," Albanese added, "I've expressed that concern to people in the media."

Ben Carroll, the state premier for Victoria where Wangaratta is located, said he was "appalled" by the attack, adding: "I know how devastating this will be for the Wangaratta community and all those who Helen represents."

At a separate press conference, Albanese said everyone was "praying for her full recovery."

Although it has not yet been established whether the incident was deliberate, there has been an increase in threats and harassment targeting lawmakers and other senior public officials in Australia and elsewhere in recent years.

Haines had worked as a nurse and a midwife before entering parliament in 2019. She was known for her stance on stronger climate action.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: Ukraine got 'no warning' of Russian ballistic strikes, Zelenskyy says
entries.summary: Massive strikes overnight hit the capital Kyiv, and damaged power stations, killing at least one person and cutting power to hundreds of thousands.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Ukraine got 'no warning' of Russian ballistic strikes, Zelenskyy says

October 19, 2026

Massive strikes overnight hit the capital Kyiv, and damaged power stations, killing at least one person and cutting power to hundreds of thousands.

A barrage of Russian ballistic miles struck Kyiv and the surrounding region on Monday, killing at least one person and knocking out power to over half a million homes, Ukrainian authorities said.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Telegram that Russia had launched 16 ballistic missiles, targeting Ukraine's energy facilities, 10 of which were hit, cutting power to some 550,000 households.

The president also lamented the lack of warning from Ukraine's international partners.

"Another Russian ballistic missile attack came in several waves overnight, and once again, there was no early warning from our partners," he wrote.

Ukraine's Air Force reported strikes, which included cruise missiles and drones, hitting 25 locations. Of the 269 recorded Shahed drones deployed in the overnight attack, Ukrainian air defenses reportedly downed or suppressed 243, as well as four missiles.

Moscow says it hit drone, missile hubs in Ukraine

Russia's Defense Ministry also confirmed the "massive strikes" on Monday, saying it had targeted Ukraine with "ground-based high-precision weapons and strike drones."

The ministry said it had hit a Ukrainian data center, a logistics hub storing components for drones and cruise missiles, a train depot storing missiles and an industrial facility involved in the production of drones.

It also said it had struck a bulk carrier in the Black Sea, some 130 kilometers (80 miles) from the port of Odesa, which the ministry said had been carrying military and dual-use cargo.

Ukraine did not confirm those targets but said that a medical facility had been hit in the capital, as well as one of the city's metro stations, according to a post by the Kyiv City Military Administration on Telegram.

Kyiv, Washington disagree over pause to intelligence sharing

The overnight strikes come amid contradictory claims by both Ukraine and the US about pauses to intelligence sharing.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday that Washington had not paused some of its intelligence sharing, denying a statement Zelenskyy made on Sunday.

"I don't know where [Zelenskyy's] getting these things ​or why he's saying these things to the press. You should go back and ask him. There's been no pause," Rubio said during a visit to Uzbekistan.

"What he should ​focus on, and what we want to be focused on, is bringing an end to this war. That's what he should be focused on," he added.

Ukraine is dependent on the ability of US intelligence to spot fast-moving ballistic missiles fired by Russia. Some recent attacks have taken place without warning, Ukrainian officials have reported.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: West Bank: Israel arrests 10 suspects over settler attacks on US journalist, European diplomats
entries.summary: Israeli police made the arrests following attacks on a US journalist and European diplomats in the occupied West Bank. Israeli human rights group Yesh Din has reported at least 170 settler attacks since September 27.
entries.content:
Israel

Israel arrests 10 suspects over West Bank settler violence

October 19, 2026

Israeli police made the arrests following attacks on a US journalist and European diplomats in the occupied West Bank. Israeli human rights group Yesh Din has reported at least 170 settler attacks since September 27.

Israeli police said Monday they had arrested 10 suspects over settler violence in the occupied West Bank, including attacks on a US photojournalist and European diplomats.

Masked settlers were filmed assaulting The Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine on Friday while she was covering a Palestinian olive harvest, leaving her with broken vertebrae.

The following day, settlers attacked a convoy of European diplomats and French mayor Bernard Baudoux, who was visiting the West Bank to help with the harvest.

The incidents drew condemnation from the United States, France, Belgium and Poland.

Israeli police said the investigation was ongoing, while Israeli media reported that the Shin Bet domestic security service was involved.

What did the authorities say?

Major General Moshe Finchi, the Israeli police's West Bank commander, said "an arrest operation was conducted before dawn" following "the severe incidents of violence over the past weekend, including the assault of a media worker and the suspected attacks on foreign civilians."

Foreign Minister ⁠Gideon Saar and the Israeli military have blamed "Israeli rioters" for the attacks on the diplomats.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, however, said the diplomats entered a "sensitive area with a history of confrontations without prior coordination" ⁠with the Israeli military. He added that the facts of the attack on ⁠Levine were "unclear."

The attacks came ahead of the crucial October 27 elections for Netanyahu.

Will the Israeli settlers face prosecution?

Settler violence against Palestinians has surged, with at least 170 attacks reported since September 27, according to Israeli human rights group Yesh Din.

DW's correspondent in Jerusalem, Tania Kraemer, said Palestinians, journalists and international observers have little confidence that the arrests will lead to charges against the alleged perpetrators.

Citing a study of Israeli police investigations into violence against Palestinians in the West Bank by Yesh Din, Kraemer said only about 3% of investigations between 2005 and 2023 ended in a full or partial conviction.

More than 80% were closed because police failed to identify suspects or gather sufficient evidence, the Yesh Din report said.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: Deepfakes, bots and distrust: How AI is shaping Israel's election
entries.summary: For the first time, AI is playing a major role in Israel's elections. Observers warn that deepfakes, bots and influence campaigns could sway voters.
entries.content:
Israel

Deepfakes, bots and distrust: How AI is shaping Israel's election

October 19, 2026

For the first time, AI is playing a major role in Israel's elections. Observers warn that deepfakes, bots and influence campaigns could sway voters.

In a 19-second clipposted to X, Gadi Eisenkot, a candidate for prime minister, stands with his arms outstretched and a huge smile on his face. In slow motion, he runs through a meadow toward a person who resembles his son, wearing a shirt with the words "Israeli Unity." But Eisenkot sails past him and instead embraces Mansour Abbas, a prominent Arab politician who leads the  Ra'am party, running in the elections.

The video was posted on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's account. Opinion pollsshow Netanyahu and Eisenkot, who also happens to be a former chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces, in a tight race. The AI-generated video appears to be designed to play on anti-Arab sentiment — a big part of Netanyahu's campaign. 

The clip was viewed more than 1 million times and stirred outrage. Eisenkot's son was killed in 2023 during the Israel-Hamas war.

According to Ze Be AI, a research project of the Open University of Israel, monitoring AI content in the 2026 legislative election campaign, this clip is just one of more than 1,800 posts with AI-generated content that Netanyahu's Likud party had released throughout the election campaign by mid-October. That represents about a quarter of the Likud party social media materials analyzed by Ze Be AI.   

On October 27, Israelis will vote in an election that could oust Netanyahu from power or cement his grip on the country for the coming years. Political scientists are already calling it Israel's first AI election. Parties have been deploying AI across every aspect of campaigning — from creating outrageous videos aimed at stirring controversy to robocalling voters and unleashing bots online.

"There is a scenario where, in a strategic point shortly before the election, AI could or would be used in ways that would steer controversy that could tilt the election results," said Anat Ben-David, a media researcher leading the Ze Be AI project at the Open University of Israel.

AI videos go mainstream

Ben-David and her research team have been tracking all of the content posted on social media by politicians since the end of July. By mid-October, they had collected more than 44,000 posts across Facebook, Instagram, X and TikTok and found that over 14% of the material used AI in some way. 

A hybrid approach was most common, with AI being deployed for a part or segments of an ad: in images, music, subtitles, logos or full-fledged deepfakes.

Some fringe parties use the greatest ratio of AI in their content. But Likud is the winner by far when it comes to sheer numbers of AI use in content analyzed by the team. Netanyahu's party is followed his left-wing rivals, the Democrats, and then Eisenkot's party, Yashar — though at far lower numbers.

Israel's Central Elections Committee issued a new rule in July mandating that all AI-generated or -manipulated content in election campaigning be labeled. Beyond that, there are few limits. 

"There's no AI Act, no Digital Services Act, and the privacy law is very outdated," Ben-David said. "Then you see new [AI] uses that would be impossible to see in Europe."

Some of those uses have come from Israel's most prominent politicians.

Yair Golan, head of the Democrats, has been trying to capitalize on popular internet trends. One videolabeled as AI content features him sitting under a ceiling fan — with each rotation of the blade, his outfit changes: from an army uniform to a T-shirt with the popular slogan "bring them home now" (referring to Israeli hostages in Gaza) to a suit and tie. 

In one photorealistic AI video, posted by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich in September, Israel's attorney general and Supreme Court justices are apprehended at an anti-government protest. Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara has frequently clashed with the ruling coalition. 

And National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir shared an AI-generated video  of Palestinians being wheeled on a conveyor belt into what looks like a concentration camp. That post drew widespread condemnation, with Germany's Foreign Ministry calling it"completely unacceptable" and "abhorrent." 

The election authority has shown some willingness to intervene. In July, its chairman ordered Smotrich to take down an unlabeled AI video it called misleading.  

A new generation of robocall

It's not just deepfakes and ads: AI is also being used to reach voters directly.

Some voters are getting a new kind of AI-powered robocall — far more conversational than the robotic automated calls of the past. Nitsan Yasur, a disinformation researcher at the Israel InternetAssociation, shared a recording with DW of a four-minute phone call.

In it, a voice introduces itself as a pollster named Danielle with an Israeli polling institute and asks for his voting preferences. When Yasur asks if the voice is human, it admits, "there is no human agent on the line," before continuing to ask, "would you like to continue with the short survey?"

The bot fields several of Yasur's questions, while always steering back to who he would vote for. But when Yasur asks five times who commissioned the survey, it doesn't reveal the information. So it remains unclear whether this was part of an election campaign or a poll. What is clear is how advanced robocalling has become.

"You don't need real people making real phone calls, which are obviously limited in time and capacity," Tehilla Shwartz Altshuler, a senior fellow at the Israel Democracy Institute, told DW.

Efforts to shape what chatbots tell voters

Some Israelis are also turning to AI for advice on how to vote.

About a quarter of Israelis said they would consider using AI tools or other online services to inform their voting decisions, the Israel Internet Association found in a survey.

That raises concerns about generative engine optimization (GEO): creating online content designed to be picked up by AI chatbots and shape their answers. The Israeli government has already tapped this industry. According to filings under the Foreign Agents Registration Act, it paid a US firm to build websites meant to feed LLM systems with content supportive of the government in order to make AI chatbots more pro-Israel. 

"The same industries are going to be used now inwards in order to affect the elections," she said.

Bot accounts promote Netanyahu online

There's fake content, and then there are fake audiences. Scooper, an Israeli company specializing in media monitoring, told DW that it discovered a network of inauthentic accounts boosting Netanyahu on social media. On X, more than 1,000 new accounts have been appearing daily and immediately following the Israeli prime minister. His Instagram following has also surged in recent weeks.

About 70% of the accounts that share Netanyahu's posts on X are based outside of Israel and resemble bots, Scooper research manager Gil Feldman told DW. Feldman said the company flagged them by looking for suspicious behavior such as round-the-clock posting, recent creation dates and missing profile pictures.

And it's not just Netanyahu: The Israeli watchdog FakeReporter found a bot campaign linked to Ben-Gvir's campaign, which his office denied. FakeReporter discovered a network of more than 100 accounts, some using AI-generated images and identities, targeting Smotrich and others.

Though bot networks are nothing new, AI can make them cheaper and easier to run. And, because Israelis are early and eager adopters of new technology, Shwartz Altshuler sees the country as a test case for how AI is reshaping elections around the world.

"The whole machinery of political propaganda is becoming totally different," Shwartz Altshuler said.

Edited by: Uta Steinwehr, Chiponda Chimbelu, Joscha Weber, Shani Rozanes

entries.title: Germany news: Berlin conference seeks to drum up investment
entries.summary: The "Invest in Germany Summit" is set to kick off in Berlin as the government looks to fill gaps in public funding. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Berlin conference seeks to drum up investment

Published October 19, 2026last updated October 19, 2026

The "Invest in Germany Summit" is set to kick off in Berlin as the government looks to fill gaps in public funding. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Chancellor Friedrich Merz is to give the welcome speech at a conference aiming to boost investment in Germany
  • Operations have returned to normal after a security incident at the Leipzig/Halle airport
  • Carmaker Volkswagen is intending to freeze the salaries of many of its workers until 2030
  • The Berlin Social Democrats and Greens are to decide whether to start coalition negotiations with the Left Party after ending exploratory talks

This is a roundup of the stories from and about Germany that are hitting the headlines on Monday, October 19, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Foreign Ministry summons Iranian ambassador over planned anti-Israel attacks

Foreign Ministry summons Iranian ambassador over planned anti-Israel attacks

The Foreign Ministry has summoned Iran's ambassador after two men were convicted of preparing attacks on Jewish figures and pro-Israel targets in Germany at the behest of Tehran.

"We vehemently condemn Iran's activities. We will not allow Iran to threaten our liberal society," the ministry wrote on X.

"We do not tolerate attacks on Jewish life and those who defend it anywhere, and particularly not in Germany," it wrote.

 A Hamburg court on Thursday sentenced a 54-year-old man and a 43-year old man respectively to 8 1/2 and 4 1/2 years in prison for having spied on the president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, Josef Schuster, and Volker Beck, the president of the German-Israeli Society (DIG).

In the court's opinion, their actions were carried out in preparation for terrorist attacks, including the planned murders of Schuster and Beck.

The court said the 54-year-old, who was said to have also done the groundwork for an arson attack on a kosher food store in Berlin, received his orders directly from officers in the Quds Force.

The Quds Force is the branch of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) that is in charge of extraterritorial operations.

Skip next section Novice driver caused fence breach at Leipzig/Halle airport: Police

Novice driver caused fence breach at Leipzig/Halle airport: Police

Two men have admitted to breaking through a fence at Leipzig/Halle airport while one of them was practicing for a driving test, an incident that triggered a major security operation, police said on Monday.

The two, aged 20 and 32, have handed themselves in to police.

The mass-circulation Bild newspaper reported that the car involved, of which fragments were found at the site, was an Audi.

The airport was the site of a security scare in August, when an explosives-laden drone was found there near Ukrainian cargo planes.

German officials accused Russia of having planned an attack, something Moscow denied.

Skip next section German industry shed almost half a million jobs since 2019: Ifo Institute

German industry shed almost half a million jobs since 2019: Ifo Institute

 German industrial businesses employed some 496,000 fewer people at the end of 2025 compared to the start of 2019, according to a survey conducted by the Ifo Institute economic think tank.

The figure represents a 7.1% decline.

Worst-hit has been the automotive industry, a key sector of the German economy, where 123,500 jobs were cut both at carmakers and suppliers, a decline of 13%.

But the metals sector also saw a marked decline in the number of jobs available, dropping 115,600 workers in the period, while the machinery sector bled 64,500 positions.

At the same time, more than 2.2 million additional jobs were created in the service sector, according to Ifo.

It said 391,000 new jobs had been established in the health sector and another 357,000 in social services, including care homes.

Joachim Ragnitz, managing director at Ifo Dresden, said the figures showed an "accelerated structural shift" in Germany.

"Ironically, the very sectors that have sustained our prosperity up to now are shrinking," he said.

"The new jobs are for the most part not being created where Germany is especially productive and innovative. That may slow down our growth potential in the future."

Skip next section German woman climber dies in fall in Italy

German woman climber dies in fall in Italy

A German woman has died in a climbing accident in the Italian Alps, mountain rescuers said on Monday.

The 32-year-old woman, who was an experienced mountaineer, fell more than 50 meters (164 feet) to her death while on the Cengia dei Camosci, a difficult route on the 2,323-meter Grande Nabois mountain near the Slovenian border.

The rescue service said the accident was caused when a climbing hold gave way under the woman, who was accompanied by an Austrian fellow climber at the time.

Her body was recovered by helicopter.

Investigations are underway to clarify the exact circumstances of her death.

Skip next section Volkswagen plans to freeze pay till 2030: works council

Volkswagen plans to freeze pay till 2030: works council

Carmaker Volkswagen intends to freeze the salaries of some 660,000 employees worldwide until 2030 as the company, along with the entire car industry, faces a range of challenges that have impacted its profits.

Trade union IG Metall confirmed earlier media reports of the plans, citing information given to employees by the works council.

The works council described the plans as unrealistic and said there would be considerable resistance to them.

If the company does implement them, employees could lose an estimated 10% of their purchasing power by the end of the decade.

The news comes after VW decided in September to cut 50,000 jobs worldwide in the coming years in addition to the reduction of 50,000 positions that had already been agreed.

Four plants in Germany are also at risk of being closed between 2031 and 2034.

Skip next section Women well behind men in leadership positions: Destatis

Women well behind men in leadership positions: Destatis

Less than a third of leadership positions in Germany are held by women, a lower level than the EU average, statistics released on Monday showed.

According to the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), citing figures from the EU statistics authority Eurostat, women held just 30.3% of leadership positions in Germany, compared with 35.9% in the whole of the EU.

Only Cyprus, Italy and the Netherlands have lower rates than Germany in the bloc, while Sweden has the highest, at 44.4%, followed by Latvia, Estonia and Poland.

"The low proportion of women in leadership positions in Germany is particularly striking, as almost as many women as men are employed here," Destatis said, comparing the situation with Italy, which has almost the same level of female leadership but a much lower rate of female employment overall.

Destatis defines leadership positions as those involving the management of small companies, the management of large companies or departments within them and high administrative posts.

Skip next section Merz to open investment conference

Merz to open investment conference

A two-day conference entitled "Invest in Germany Summit" is to begin on Monday evening in Berlin as the government seeks to shore up public-sector spending with private money.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz will deliver the opening speech at the conference, which will be attended by an expected 200 representatives from large German and international companies.

The CEO of the US chip manufacturer Nvidia, Jensen Huang, is to be one of the key guests at the conference.

The German government is looking to cooperate strongly with the company, whose products are central to the boom in artificial intelligence, in a bid to help Germany catch up in the sector.

Don't expect too much: Economic institute

The German Economic Institute (IW) has, however, warned against any too high expectations from the summit, saying that high costs for labor, energy and bureaucracy in Germany were a deterrent to investment in the country.

"It would be naive to believe that the summit will change that in the short term. Companies don't choose Germany because of a promotional event. What matters is whether they can make money here," IW director Michael Hüther told the DPA news agency.

He said it would be more effective if the government were to swiftly implement its reform agenda.

A study by Allianz Research has shown that investment in Germany fell by 6.4% between 2019 and 2025, while it grew by 6.7% in the rest of the eurozone and a whole 20.2% in the US.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

The DW newsroom in Bonn bids guten Tag to all its faithful readers at the start of a new week!

Today, we will be looking at a conference in Berlin that will seek to attract private investment in Germany to help make the country fit for the future, with the field of artificial intelligence a key focus.

New statistics are also to be released on Monday on women in leadership and government positions in Germany and the EU in 2025.

And the Leipzig/Halle airport has resumed normal operations after a security incident involving a breached fence triggered a large-scale police operation.

This occurred just weeks after an explosives-laden drone that German officials believe was intended to carry out an attack on behalf of Russia was found at the airport.

Read on for more on these and other stories connected with all things German.

entries.title: India news: CJP alleges 'deliberate' delay in leaders' release
entries.summary: CJP leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were due to be released on Sunday. The judge in the case has recused himself after claiming that he was threatened. DW has more.
entries.content:
Asia

India news: CJP alleges 'deliberate' delay in leaders' release

Published October 19, 2026last updated October 19, 2026

CJP leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were due to be released on Sunday. The judge in the case has recused himself after claiming that he was threatened. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • The Delhi Police has filed a case over alleged threats to the judge overseeing CJP leader's bail hearings
  • Organized crime boss Lawrence Bishnoi's gang claims attack on Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff
  • Jamia Millia Islamia University has constituted a panel to look into students' demand for a union

Here's a roundup of our coverage from India on Monday, October 19:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Rubio says India-US trade deal one of the factors behind Russian sanctions waiver

Rubio says India-US trade deal one of the factors behind Russian sanctions waiver

Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Monday said that the US had considered the India-US trade deal when deciding to to waive sanctions against Russian oil .

Rubio added that the US-India deal was "close to finalizing."

The statement came a day before Rubio visits India, and days after the US government signed a deal to buy Russian oil and announced a pause on sanctions on Russia.

Rubio cited the importance of India's importance as an ally to the US and its dependence on Russian oil as he defended President Donald Trump's decision to waive sanctions on Russian oil imports.

"We have had to waive sanctions over the past few months, looking at the global supplies, looking at global prices, and the impact it was having on other countries," he said during a press conference in Uzbekistan.

Rubio is due to meet with Indian External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar in Mumbai on Tuesday.

Skip next section Omar Abdullah demands action over attack on Kashmir-bound bus

Omar Abdullah demands action over attack on Kashmir-bound bus

Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister Omar Abdullah has condemned the attack on a Srinagar-bound bus in Haryana on Saturday.

According to Indian media reports, he wrote to the Haryana government, which has assured him that stringent action would be taken.

"This unfortunate incident should never have taken place. I hope the Haryana government led by Nayab Singh Saini and Haryana police catch the culprits & take action to ensure these things don’t happen again," Abdullah said in a post on X.

The bus, which was traveling from Delhi to Srinagar on Saturday, was reportedly attacked in the state of Haryana, outside the capital, by unidentified persons.

They allegedly pelted it with stones, leaving an elderly Kashmiri passenger injured.

Skip next section Hunger strike over restoration of students' union at Jamia University enters seventh day

Hunger strike over restoration of students' union at Jamia University enters seventh day

Students demanding the restoration of the students' union at Muslim-minority Jamia Millia University in New Delhi have continued their hunger strike for the seventh day. 

The students have been on an indefinite hunger strike since October 12.

Last week, tensions escalated at the university as Delhi police tried to thwart the protests by allegedly detaining students. Some students also alleged they were assaulted by the police personnel.

The protesting students, as reported by The New Indian Express newspaper, have three demands: the immediate reinstatement of the Jamia Millia Islamia Students Union (JMISU), the revocation of all ongoing disciplinary action against students involved in the movement and an end to further punitive measures.

The university administration late Sunday night formed a seven-member committee to look into the demands of the students, in a move aimed at restoring normalcy on campus.

The JMISU was disbanded by the university in 2006.

Skip next section Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff shot at in Mumbai, gunmen arrested

Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff shot at in Mumbai, gunmen arrested

Three people were arrested in the western state of Rajasthan on Monday, in connection with the shooting at Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff, police said. 

Five rounds were allegedly fired at Shroff's vehicle in Mumbai around 7 p.m. local time on Sunday. While Shroff escaped unhurt, his driver Firdosh and a bystander, Umesh Chavan, sustained bullet injuries, according to a report by The Indian Express newspaper.

The Bishnoi gang, who is accused of involvement in the 2023 killing of Sikh separatist Hardeep Singh Nijjar in Canada, has claimed responsibility for the attack.

In an audio message, Anil Pandit — linked to the Bishnoi gang — reportedly said he, along with Harman Sandhu, was behind the attack.

However, the Mumbai Police has not confirmed the Bishnoi gang's alleged involvement in the case.

Pandit reportredly warned that unless the actors stop working with Bollywood actor Salman Khan, the attacks will continue. "Anyone in the Mumbai film industry who does not listen to us or works with Salman Khan will be next. Wait and watch."

The attack on Shroff is the latest in a series of incidents of threats and violence allegedly connected to the Bishnoi gang, against Bollywood personalities over their links with Salman Khan.

The feud between Salman Khan and Lawrence Bishnoi dates back to 1998. It began with the poaching of two blackbuck antelopes, which is a sacred species to the Bishnoi community, to which Lawrence Bishnoi belongs.

Skip next section CJP leaders remain in custody, magistrate alleges threat to life

CJP leaders remain in custody, magistrate alleges threat to life

The release of Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leaders Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, who were sent to five days of judicial custody on October 14 for entering Jantar Mantar, has been delayed.

Jantar Mantar has been a prominent protest site in the heart of Delhi for decades. However, Delhi police blocked it amid heavy barricading and deployment.

The duo's judicial custody was supposed to end on Sunday, but their bail hearing was stalled after the special executive magistrate failed to arrive at the scheduled time and later recused himself, citing a threat to his life.

The Delhi Police have registered a case against unknown persons for threatening the magistrate in connection with Ranka and Das's bails.

According to The Times of India, police sources said the magistrate is being pressured to release Ranka and Das without delay.

CJP's legal affairs chief, Ratna Singh, has alleged a "deliberate use of delaying tactics" to keep Das and Ranka "behind bars."

On Sunday, Singh said they had completed every required procedure and were "merely waiting for formal approval."

The CJP were detained amid calls for protests demanding the removal of top election official Gyanesh Kumar over his alleged involvement in electroal irregularities and mass deletions from voter rolls.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Hello! This is Midhat reporting from DW's New Delhi bureau, bringing you all the latest buzz from India.

Much like some other parts of the world, India is living through a tense political moment, with mass public pushback against the government.

The youth-led protests called by the Cockroach Janta Party were met with an unprecedented police crackdown on protesters in the past week, with the party's leaders being detained. 

While CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke was released on Saturday, other prominent leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka remain in judicial custody.

Protests were also held at the Muslim-minority university Jamia Millia Islamia over restoration of the students' union.

Meanwhile, Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff was shot at by unidentified assailants in Mumbai. The gang ran by Lawrence Bishnoi — the gangster who is accused of involvement in the 2023 killing of Sikh separatist Hardeep Singh Nijjar in Canada — has claimed the attack.

Stay tuned with us as we bring you more updates from India.
